title: A Cheap Supplement Just Made Diabetic Hearts 15 Per Cent More Efficient. South Asians Should Pay Attention.
excerpt: University of Leeds researchers found that mitoquinone reversed early signs of heart damage in Type 2 diabetes patients within four months. A larger trial is next.
body:
A low-cost antioxidant supplement called mitoquinone made the hearts of people with Type 2 diabetes work 15 per cent more efficiently in just four months, according to a new study from the University of Leeds. The findings, presented at the British Cardiovascular Society conference in Manchester, suggest that a daily capsule costing a few pence could one day help prevent the cascade from diabetes to heart failure.

The trial enrolled 70 adults with Type 2 diabetes who had no prior diagnosis of heart disease. Half received a daily 40-milligram dose of mitoquinone — sold commercially as MitoQ — on top of their standard diabetes treatment. The other half continued with standard care alone. After four months, cardiac MRI scans revealed that the supplement group's hearts were significantly better at converting fuel into mechanical work.

## How It Works

Mitoquinone is a synthetic cousin of coenzyme Q10, a naturally occurring molecule that helps mitochondria — the energy factories inside every cell — produce the chemical fuel that powers the body. What makes mitoquinone different is its ability to penetrate directly into mitochondria, where it neutralises the damaging molecules known as reactive oxygen species.

In diabetes, chronically high blood sugar drives mitochondria to produce excess reactive oxygen species, gradually poisoning the heart muscle from within. The heart, which beats roughly 100,000 times a day and has virtually no capacity to store energy, is uniquely vulnerable to this kind of metabolic stress. Over years, the damage accumulates until the heart can no longer pump blood effectively — a condition known as heart failure.

The Leeds team's hypothesis was straightforward: if you could reduce oxidative stress inside cardiac mitochondria, you might slow or reverse the early stages of this process before clinical symptoms appear.

## The Numbers That Matter

The study found that mitoquinone improved myocardial energetic efficiency — the ratio of energy produced to energy consumed by the heart — by approximately 15 per cent at rest. No participants in either group developed serious cardiac events during the trial, though the researchers emphasised that the study was small and short.

"This is the first evidence in humans that targeting mitochondrial oxidative stress can meaningfully improve how the diabetic heart handles energy," said the study's lead investigator. The team is now planning a much larger, multi-year trial to determine whether these improvements translate into fewer heart failure diagnoses and better survival.

## A Condition That Hits South Asians Hardest

Heart failure is the most common initial presentation of cardiovascular disease in people with diabetes, and South Asians face the sharpest end of this risk. Studies consistently show that people of South Asian descent develop Type 2 diabetes at rates three to five times higher than white European populations, often a decade earlier in life. The UK alone has 5.8 million people living with diabetes, and the community burden among British Indians, Pakistanis, and Bangladeshis is disproportionately high.

In the United States, first-generation Indian immigrants frequently develop insulin resistance in their 30s and 40s, a pattern driven by genetic predisposition, visceral fat distribution, and the metabolic toll of dietary transition. Once diabetes takes hold, the risk of heart failure is up to five times greater than in the general population. And once heart failure develops, outcomes are significantly worse.

## What This Does Not Mean Yet

Mitoquinone is widely available as a dietary supplement and is generally considered safe at the doses used in this study. But the Leeds researchers cautioned strongly against treating these early results as a green light to self-medicate. The trial was designed to test a biological mechanism, not to establish clinical guidelines. A much larger study with longer follow-up is needed before any medical body would consider recommending it as part of diabetes care.

Still, for a community that bears a disproportionate burden of both diabetes and its cardiac consequences, the prospect of a simple, affordable intervention that targets the disease at its metabolic root is worth watching closely. The supplement costs less than a daily cup of coffee. The question now is whether it can deliver protection that lasts.
